metadata.description: Griewank's AD paper develops reverse-mode automatic differentiation as a general technique with cost bounded by a constant times the function-evaluation cost; Rumelhart-Hinton-Williams' backpropagation is precisely the instantiation of reverse-mode AD on a layered feedforward network with a sum-of-squares loss. Same algorithmic method (reverse accumulation of derivatives via the transposed chain rule), distinct application domains (general scientific computing vs neural-network learning). Both papers are PDF-fallback extractions, so name/type carry more weight than literal LaTeX.

matches.explanation: Griewank's 'Original Program (sequential factorable representation)' models a function as a sequential program $x_i = f_i\langle x_j\rangle_{j\in\mathcal{J}_i}$ over intermediate scalars. RHW's layered feed-forward network is a particular instance of this: each unit $j$ in a layer has elementary functions $x_j = \sum_i y_i w_{ji}$ (linear input combination) followed by $y_j = 1/(1+e^{-x_j})$ (sigmoid). The factorable-program abstraction in 388 specializes here to the linear-then-sigmoid composition of a multilayer net.

388's computational graph (a DAG of intermediate variables with arcs labelled by local partials $\partial f_i/\partial x_j$) is the general structure that the layered network of 389 instantiates. RHW's network is a particular layered DAG with weights $w_{ji}$ as the arc labels in the linear sub-step; arcs respect the layer order forbidding within-layer or top-down connections.

388's adjoint quantity $\bar{x}_i \equiv \partial x_m/\partial x_i$ is exactly RHW's error derivative $\partial E/\partial y_i$ (and $\partial E/\partial x_j$ for the pre-activation). EP389.1 sets the output-layer adjoint $\partial E/\partial y_j = y_j - d_j$ (analogue of $\bar{x}_m = 1$ seeded for the scalar output, here the squared-error loss), EP389.2 and EP389.4 propagate the adjoint backward via the chain rule. These are the same mathematical objects under different naming conventions.

388's reverse-mode adjoint recursion $\bar{x}_j = \sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_j} (\partial f_i/\partial x_j)\,\bar{x}_i$ is identical in content to RHW's back-propagated error $\partial E/\partial y_i = \sum_j (\partial E/\partial x_j)\,w_{ji}$, where $w_{ji} = \partial x_j/\partial y_i$ is the local partial of the linear sub-step. Same transposed chain-rule formula.

RHW's weight-derivative formula $\partial E/\partial w_{ji} = (\partial E/\partial x_j)\,y_i$ is the special case of the reverse-mode adjoint recursion (388's EP388.2) applied to the linear sub-step $x_j = \sum_i y_i w_{ji}$, where the local partial with respect to a parameter is $\partial x_j/\partial w_{ji} = y_i$. Same transposed chain rule, instantiated for a learnable parameter rather than an intermediate variable.

388's general Reverse Extension (forward sweep computing intermediate values, then reverse sweep accumulating adjoints via the transposed chain rule) is exactly RHW's back-propagation algorithm specialized to a layered network with sum-of-squares loss. The two-pass structure, the sequencing of intermediate-value storage and reverse adjoint update, and the resulting gradient-computation cost are the same. This is the central correspondence supporting the SM relation: backprop IS reverse-mode AD applied to neural nets.

Composite L2 alignment of the inner steps of the two algorithms (parent match emitted above as AP388.4 ↔ AP389.1). 388's forward sweep (ASP388.1) corresponds to RHW's forward pass (ASP389.2); 388's adjoint initialization (ASP388.2) corresponds to seeding the output-layer error $\partial E/\partial y_j = y_j - d_j$ (ASP389.3); 388's reverse sweep (ASP388.3) corresponds to RHW's backward propagation step (ASP389.4) and weight-gradient computation (ASP389.5); 388's return of the gradient (ASP388.4) corresponds to extracting $\partial E/\partial w_{ji}$. The step DAGs match one-for-one with the obvious specialization to the linear-then-sigmoid layered structure.
Forward-mode AD has no counterpart in RHW. RHW use only the reverse mode (backpropagation); they never discuss forward-mode propagation of gradient vectors.
Forward-mode AD specialized to the product function (Speelpenning's pedagogical example) has no analog in RHW, who do not consider this baseline.

Reverse-mode AD specialized to the product function (Speelpenning's trick) is a tiny pedagogical instance of the same method that RHW deploy in full generality on layered nets; the structural correspondence is the two-sweep forward-then-reverse pattern. Match is weaker than AP388.4 ↔ AP389.1 because the test function differs.

Wolfe's cheap-gradient theorem ($q\{f\} \le 5$ uniformly in $n$) is the central complexity-theoretic claim of 388. RHW state no analogous bound; they describe backprop operationally without proving its cost relative to the forward pass. This is a paper-original contribution of 388 with no counterpart in 389.
Composition closure of $Q\{f\}$ is a structural complexity result of 388 with no counterpart in RHW, who do not analyze cost-closure properties of their procedure.
The work-ratio definition $q\{f\}$ measures the gradient-vs-function cost ratio; RHW have no cost-analysis machinery, so this concept has no analog.
Generalized work ratio $Q\{f\}$ for the gradient-update increment has no counterpart in RHW.
The Wolfe 1982 cheap-gradient problem (bound the cost of gradient evaluation by a constant times function cost) is not posed by RHW; their problem is about learning, not gradient complexity.

The credit-assignment / hidden-representation learning problem (find weights so outputs match targets despite no targets for hidden units) is the motivating problem of RHW and has no analog in Griewank's AD paper.
Bias as an extra unit with constant input 1 is a neural-network modeling convention specific to RHW; 388's general factorable-program framework does not single it out.
Sum-of-squares total error $E = \tfrac{1}{2}\sum_c\sum_j (y_{j,c}-d_{j,c})^2$ is RHW's loss; 388 treats $f$ as a generic scalar function, so there is no specific loss object on the AD side.
Vanilla gradient-descent update $\Delta w = -\varepsilon\,\partial E/\partial w$ is the optimization step in RHW; Griewank's paper computes gradients but does not prescribe an optimization update.
Momentum update $\Delta w(t) = -\varepsilon\,\partial E/\partial w(t) + \alpha\,\Delta w(t-1)$ is an optimization heuristic specific to RHW with no analog in 388.
Forward-mode work bound is a cost formula tied to forward AD; not applicable in RHW.
Hessian forward-mode recursion is a second-order construction of 388; RHW work only with first-order gradients.
Hessian-vector reverse bound $n\bar{Q}^2$ is a second-order cost result of 388; no counterpart in RHW.
Operation-counting bound $\bar{Q} \le 5$ for multiplication; cost-analysis specific to 388.
Local error-propagation bound is a numerical-analysis result of 388; RHW do not address rounding-error analysis.

MACSYMA-generated FORTRAN gradient code is an illustrative listing in 388 demonstrating the unwieldy output of symbolic differentiation; no counterpart in RHW, who do not benchmark against symbolic systems.
Storage-vs-time tradeoff for reverse mode (need to store all forward intermediates) is discussed in 388 but not in RHW.
Forward-mode linear-growth lower bound is part of 388's contrast between forward and reverse modes; absent from RHW.
ODE-adjoint correspondence is a domain-bridging remark in 388 with no analog in RHW.
Higher-derivative-vector cost bound $5^{1+p}$ is a higher-order complexity result of 388; absent from RHW.
Additivity of computational work is an assumption used in 388's complexity analysis; no counterpart in RHW.

Multi-output reverse increment $g = \bar{g} + \gamma\nabla f$ is a generalization of the reverse pass used to prove composition closure in 388; absent in RHW (which seeds only $\partial E/\partial y_j$ at the output).
Proof of $\bar{Q}\le 5$ via per-operation count is a complexity-theoretic argument of 388; RHW prove no such bound.
Proof of composition closure of $Q\{f\}$ is specific to 388's complexity framework.
Open problem on combinatorial graph optimization for AD is specific to 388.
Open problem on optimal storage / splines for ODE-defined $f$ is specific to 388.
Open problem on best derivative-matrix strategy for vector-valued $F$ is specific to 388.
